## Summary

I reviewed all 10 source files in the repository. Two exploitable findings:

**1. Open redirect (`src/routes/continue.js`) — HIGH**
The `/continue` route reflects `req.query.returnTo` verbatim into `res.redirect` with no validation. An attacker can craft `/continue?returnTo=https://evil.com` to redirect users from the trusted domain to an attacker-controlled site — exploitable for phishing.

**2. SSRF (`src/routes/preview.js`, `src/policy/outbound.js`, `src/http/client.js`) — HIGH**
The `/preview` route's allow-list uses `url.startsWith('https://trusted.example.test')`, which is bypassable. I verified in Node that `https://trusted.example.test@evil.com/x` passes the check (`startsWith=true`) but resolves to hostname `evil.com` (the trusted prefix is reinterpreted as URL userinfo), and `https://trusted.example.test.evil.com/x` also passes while resolving to a different host. Combined with `followRedirects: true` in the HTTP client, the server can be coerced into fetching arbitrary URLs including internal hosts.

**Reviewed and determined NOT exploitable:**
- `src/routes/avatar.js` + `src/policy/origin.js`: uses strict URL parsing (protocol, hostname, port equality) and `redirect: 'manual'` — verified it rejects all bypass attempts.
- `src/commands/thumbnail.js`: `spawn` with `shell: false` and arg array — no command injection; not wired to any route.
- `src/logging.js`, `src/config.js`: no exploitable issues.
- No `package.json`/lockfile present, so no `vulnerable-dependency` finding applies.
